en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 30: Cūḷasāropamasutta (The Shorter Discourse on the Simile of the Heartwood)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the brahmin Piṅgalakoccha approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the brahmin Piṅgalakoccha said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, as for those ascetics and brahmins who have an order, a following, and are teachers of a group; who are well-known and famous founders of sects,
highly regarded by the multitude— namely, Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita Kesakambala, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta, and Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta—
did they all claim super-knowledge according to their own assertions, or did none of them claim super-knowledge, or did some claim it while others did not?”
“Enough, brahmin, let this be—
whether all of them have directly known it by their own declaration, or whether none of them have directly known it, or whether some have directly known it and some have not.
I will teach you the Dhamma, brahmin.”
“Listen to this, and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, sir,” the brahmin Piṅgalakoccha replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Just as if, brahmin, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood,
were to pass right by a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and having bypassed the heartwood, bypassed the sapwood, bypassed the bark, and bypassed the inner bark,
he were to cut off the branches and foliage and depart, thinking he had found ‘heartwood.’”
A man with good eyesight, seeing him, would say:

"Truly, this worthy man did not recognize the heartwood, he did not recognize the sapwood, he did not recognize the bark, he did not recognize the inner bark, nor did he recognize the twigs and leaves.
For this worthy man, seeking heartwood, searching for heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, [has taken] from a great tree..."
"Suppose a man, passing over the heartwood of a standing tree that possesses heartwood, passes over the sapwood, passes over the bark, and passes over the inner bark;
having cut off the branches and foliage, he takes them and departs, thinking, 'This is heartwood.
Whatever purpose he has to serve with heartwood, he will not achieve that goal."
Or again, brahmin, it is as if a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood,
were to pass right by the heartwood of a large standing tree possessed of heartwood, and passing by the sapwood, passing by the bark,
were to cut off the outer shell and take it away, thinking, "This is heartwood."
A man with good eyesight, seeing this, would say:

"Truly, this worthy man did not recognize the heartwood, he did not recognize the sapwood, he did not recognize the bark, he did not recognize the inner bark, nor did he recognize the branches and foliage.
For this worthy man, seeking heartwood, searching for heartwood, and wandering in search of heartwood, [approached] a great tree..."

"Suppose a man were to pass by a standing tree possessed of heartwood, and having bypassed the heartwood, bypassed the sapwood, and bypassed the bark, he were to cut off the outer shell and take it away,
thinking, 'This is heartwood. Whatever purpose there might be for heartwood, that purpose he would not achieve with what he has taken."
Or again, brahmin, it is as if a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood,
were to pass right by the heartwood of a large standing tree possessed of heartwood, and passing over the heartwood and the sapwood,
were to cut off the bark and take it away, thinking, "This is heartwood."
A man with good eyesight, seeing him, would say:

"Truly, this worthy man did not recognize the heartwood, he did not recognize the sapwood, he did not recognize the bark, he did not recognize the inner bark, and he did not recognize the twigs and leaves.
For this worthy man, seeking heartwood, searching for heartwood, and wandering in search of heartwood, [approached] a great tree..."
"Passing over the heartwood of a standing tree that possesses heartwood, and passing over the sapwood as well, he cuts away the bark, takes it, and departs, thinking, 'This is the heartwood.
Whatever purpose there might be for the heartwood, that purpose he will not achieve."
Or again, brahmin, it is as if a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood,
were to pass right by a great standing tree possessed of heartwood, and cutting away the sapwood, were to take it and depart,
thinking he had obtained "heartwood."
A man with good eyesight, seeing him, would say:

"Truly, this gentleman did not recognize the heartwood, he did not recognize the sapwood, he did not recognize the bark, he did not recognize the inner bark, and he did not recognize the twigs and leaves.

For this gentleman, seeking heartwood, searching for heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, passed right by the heartwood of this great standing tree possessed of heartwood; instead, having cut off the sapwood, he has departed taking it, thinking, 'This is heartwood.'"
"And whatever purpose he has for the heartwood, that purpose he will not achieve.

Or again, brahmin, it is as if a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to cut down the very heartwood of a large standing tree possessed of heartwood, take it away, and depart, knowing it to be "heartwood.
Then a person with vision, seeing him, would say this:
‘This worthy man has surely recognized the heartwood; he has recognized the sapwood, the bark, the inner bark, and the twigs and leaves.

For this worthy man, seeking heartwood, searching for heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, having cut down the very heartwood of a great standing tree possessed of heartwood, has taken it and departed, knowing it to be “heartwood.
Whatever purpose there may be to be served by heartwood, he will experience that benefit.’”
In the same way, brahmin, here a certain person goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
"I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs.
Immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering, perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned."
Having thus gone forth, he produces gain, honor, and fame.
He becomes elated by that gain, honor, and fame, his purpose fulfilled.
On account of that gain, honor, and fame, he exalts himself and disparages others:
‘I possess gain, honor, and renown, whereas these other bhikkhus are unknown and of little influence.

Because of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not generate desire or exert effort for the realization of those states that are higher and more sublime than them; he remains sluggish in his conduct and lax.
Just as if, brahmin, that man who needed heartwood, was seeking heartwood, and was wandering in search of heartwood, [from] a great...
Suppose a man, passing over the heartwood of a standing tree that possesses heartwood, passes over the sapwood, passes over the bark, and passes over the inner bark;
having cut off the branches and foliage, he takes them away thinking they are "heartwood.
Whatever purpose there might be for heartwood, he will not achieve that aim.
“Brahmin, I say that this person is just like that.
But here, brahmin, a certain person goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
‘I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs; immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering.’”
‘Perhaps an end might be made of this entire mass of suffering.
Having thus gone forth, he generates gain, honor, and fame.
Because of that gain, honor, and fame, he is not satisfied and his purpose is not fulfilled.
Thus, because of that gain, honor, and fame, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.

And regarding those other qualities which are higher and more sublime than gain, honor, and fame, he generates desire for the realization of those qualities; he strives and is unshrunken and untiring in his conduct.
He achieves perfection in virtue.
Thus, he is satisfied with that perfection of virtue and his intention is fulfilled.
On account of that perfection of virtue, he exalts himself and disparages others, thinking:
"I am virtuous and of good character, whereas these other bhikkhus are immoral and of evil character."

Furthermore, regarding those other qualities that are higher and more sublime than the perfection of virtue, he does not generate desire for the realization of those qualities, nor does he strive; he is sluggish in his conduct and lax.

Just as if, brahmin, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to pass right by a great standing tree possessed of heartwood, passing over the heartwood, passing over the sapwood, and passing over the bark...
Having cut off the outer bark and taken it away, he departs thinking, "This is the heartwood.
Yet he will not achieve the purpose for which heartwood is required.
It is in this way, brahmin, that I describe this person.
But here, brahmin, a certain person goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
"I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs.
Immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering, perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be made known."
Having thus gone forth, he generates gain, honor, and fame.
He is not satisfied with that gain, honor, and fame, nor is his purpose fulfilled by it.
On account of that gain, honor, and fame, he does not exalt himself or disparage others.
And regarding gain, honor, and fame, he generates desire, exerts himself, and remains unshrunken and untiring in order to realize those other states that are higher and more sublime than them.
He achieves perfection in virtue.
He is satisfied with that perfection in virtue, yet his intention is not yet fulfilled.
Thus, because of that perfection of virtue, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.

And regarding those other qualities which are higher and more sublime than the perfection of virtue, he generates desire for the realization of those qualities; he strives, and he is unshrunken in his conduct and not lax.
He achieves the perfection of concentration.
Thus, being satisfied with that perfection of concentration, his intention is fulfilled.
On account of that perfection of concentration, he exalts himself and disparages others, thinking:
"I am concentrated, one-pointed in mind; but these other bhikkhus are unconcentrated, with wandering minds."

And regarding those other states that are more excellent and more sublime than the perfection of concentration, he does not generate desire for the realization of those states, nor does he strive; he remains sluggish in his conduct and lax.

Just as if, brahmin, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to pass right over the heartwood of a large standing tree possessed of heartwood, and passing over the sapwood, were to cut off the bark and take it away.
Having departed, he thinks, "This is worthless.
Whatever purpose there might be in using what is substantial for that which is substantial, he will not achieve that goal.
I say, brahmin, that this person is just like that.
But here, brahmin, a certain person goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
"I am immersed in birth, aging, and death...
[and so on] ...may the making of an end be known."
Having thus gone forth, he produces gain, honor, and renown.
He is not satisfied with that gain, honor, and renown, nor does his aspiration reach fulfillment.
On account of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not exalt himself or disparage others.
And with regard to gain, honor, and fame, he generates desire, exerts himself, and remains untiring and unremiss in order to realize those other states that are higher and more sublime than them.
He achieves perfection in virtue.
He is satisfied with that perfection in virtue, yet his aspiration is not yet fulfilled.
Thus, on account of that perfection of virtue, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.

And regarding those other qualities which are higher and more sublime than the perfection of virtue, he generates desire for the realization of those qualities; he strives, and he conducts himself without shrinking back and without laxity.
He thus achieves the perfection of concentration.
Thus, he is satisfied with that perfection of concentration, yet his intention is not yet fulfilled.
On account of that perfection of concentration, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.

And regarding those other states that are higher and more sublime than the perfection of concentration, he generates desire for the realization of those states; he strives, and he conducts himself without shrinking back and without slackening.
Thus he attains knowledge and vision.
He becomes satisfied with that knowledge and vision, his purpose fulfilled.
On account of that knowledge and vision, he exalts himself and disparages others:
‘I dwell knowing and seeing, whereas these other bhikkhus dwell unknowing and unseeing.
Yet he does not generate desire or exert effort for the realization of those other states that are higher and more sublime than his knowledge and vision; he remains sluggish in his conduct and lax.
Just as if, brahmin, that man who needs heartwood, seeks heartwood, and wanders in search of heartwood, [were to come upon] a great...
“Just as if someone were to pass by a standing tree possessed of heartwood, and having cut through the sapwood,
take it away thinking it was ‘heartwood,’ yet he would not achieve the purpose for which heartwood is required—
such, O Brahmin, do I say this person is.”
But here, brahmin, a certain person goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
"I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs.
Immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering, perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be made known."
Having thus gone forth, he produces gain, honor, and fame.
He is not elated by that gain, honor, and fame, nor is his purpose fulfilled thereby.
On account of that gain, honor, and fame, he does not exalt himself or disparage others.
And with regard to gain, honor, and fame, he generates desire, exerts effort, and remains unshrunken and untiring for the realization of those other states that are higher and more sublime than them.
He achieves perfection in virtue.
He is satisfied with that perfection in virtue, yet his aspiration is not yet fulfilled.
Thus, on account of that perfection of virtue, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.

And regarding those other qualities which are higher and more sublime than the perfection of virtue, he generates desire for the realization of those qualities; he strives, and he conducts himself without shrinking back and without laxity.
He thus achieves the perfection of concentration.
Thus, he is satisfied with that perfection of concentration, yet his intention is not yet fulfilled.
On account of that perfection of concentration, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.

And regarding those other states which are higher and more sublime than the perfection of concentration, he generates desire for the realization of those states; he strives, and he remains unshrunken and untiring in his conduct.
Thus he attains knowledge and vision.
He is satisfied with that knowledge and vision, yet his intention is not yet fulfilled.
Because of that knowledge and vision, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.
And with regard to those other qualities that are higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision, he generates desire for their realization; he exerts himself, and he is untiring and not lax.
And what, brahmin, are those qualities higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision?

Here, brahmin, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
“This too, brahmin, is a state that is higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

Furthermore, brahmin, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
This too, brahmin, is a state that is higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.”
Furthermore, brahmin, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells equanimous and mindful, clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body;
he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous."
This too, brahmin, is a state that is more excellent and more sublime than knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, brahmin, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief,
a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
This too, brahmin, is a state that is higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

Furthermore, brahmin, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] ‘space is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
This too, brahmin, is a state that is higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, brahmin, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking ‘consciousness is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
This too, brahmin, is a state that is higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, brahmin, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking ‘there is nothing,’ a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
This too, brahmin, is a state that is more excellent and more sublime than knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, brahmin, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This too, brahmin, is a state that is more excellent and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

Furthermore, brahmin, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling; and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
This too, brahmin, is a state that is higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.
These, brahmin, are states that are higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

"Just as if, brahmin, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to cut down the very heartwood of a great standing tree possessed of heartwood, take it away, and depart knowing it to be 'heartwood';
and whatever purpose he had to be served by heartwood,
that purpose he would accomplish with it— I say, brahmin, that this person is just like that."

“Thus, brahmin, this holy life does not have gain, honor, and renown as its benefit; it does not have the perfection of virtue as its benefit; it does not have the perfection of concentration as its benefit; nor does it have knowledge and vision as its benefit.
But rather, brahmin, this unshakable liberation of mind—this is the purpose of this holy life, this is its essence, this is its consummation.”
When this was said, the brahmin Piṅgalakoccha said to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… [as before] … May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.”
The Cūḷasāropama Sutta, the tenth, is finished.
The Third Chapter on Similes is finished.
Its summary verse:
And he named Moḷiyaphaggunaritta,
who was full of merit in the Andhavana forest;
and those named Rāsika, Kaṇeru, and Mahāgaja.
Furthermore, Sārūpama was Piṅgalakoccha.
